source_text: Adhuc adiciam illam quoque partem in qua dum haereticus quasi oculo quodam gaudet proprio, ueritatis et luminis amisso, totam caecitatem sui agnoscat erroris. identidem enim et frequenter opponit quia dictum sit: sano tempore uobiscum sum, et non agnoscitis me? Philippe, qui uidit me, uidit et patrem. sed quod non intellegit, discat. culpatur Philippus, et iure quidem meritoque, quia dixerit: domine, ostende nobis patrem, et sufficit nobis. quando enim ex Christo aut audierat istud aut didicerat, quasi esset pater Christus, cum contra magis, quod filius esset, non quia pater, frequenter audisset, et saepe didicisset? quod enim dixit dominus, s me cognouistis, et patrem meum cognouistis, et a modo nostis illum, et uidistis illum, non sic dixerat ut se patrem uellet intellegi, sed quoniam qui penitus et plene et cum tota fide et tota religione accessit ad dei filium, omnibus modis per ipsum filium, in quem sic credit, ad patrem peruenturus sit, eundemque uisurus. nemo enim, inquit, potest uenire ad patrem nisi per me, et ideo ad patrem deum non tantum uenturus est, et cogniturus ipsum patrem, sed etiam sic tenere debet, atque ita animo ac mente praesumere, quasi iam nouerit patrem pariter et uiderit. Saepe enim scriptura diuina, quae nondum facta pro factis annuntiat, quia sic futura sunt, et quae omnibus modis fieri habent, non quasi futura sint, praedicat, sed quasi facta sint, narrat. denique cum nondum temporibus Isaiae prophetae Christus natus fuisset, quia puer, aiebat, natus est nobis; et cum nondum accessum esset ad Mariam, e accessit ad propheten, dicebat, e concepit, et peperit filium. et cum nondum sinum patris Christus exposuisset, referebat: e uocabitur nomen eius magni consili angelus. et cum nondum fuisset passus, guas? outs, pronuntiabat, ad iugulationem adductus est. et cum adhuc crux nusquam esset, aiebat: Tota die expandi manus meas ad populum non credentem., et cum nondum iniuriose potatus fuisset, s7fz, ait, mea potauerunt me aceto. et cum spoliatus adhuc non fuisset, dicebat, super uestem meam miserunt sortem: et dinumerauerunt ossa mea: effoderunt manus meas et pedes. prouidens enim scriptura diuina pro factis dicit, quae futura scit, et pro perfectis dicit, quae futura habet, quae sine dubitatione uentura sunt. et ideo dominus in praesenti loco dicebat: a modo nostis illum, et uidistis. dicebat enim uisum iri ab eo patrem, quisquis filium secutus fuisset; non quasi filius ipse esset pater uisus, sed quod praemium consecuturus esset, quisquis illum sequi et discipulus eius esse uoluisset, ut uidere patrem posset. nam et imago est dei patris, ut his etiam illud accedat, quoniam sicut pater operatur, ita operatur et filius, et imitator est filius omnium operum paternorum; ut perinde habeat unusquisque, quasi iam uiderit patrem, dum eum uidet qui inuisibilem patrem in omnibus operibus semper imitatur. Ceterum si ipse pater est Christus, quomodo confestim adicit et dicit: gud credit in me, opera quae ego facio et ipse Faciet, et maiora his faciet, quia ego ad patrem uado? et adhuc subnectit: si diligitis me, praecepta mea seruate: et ego rogabo patrem, et alium aduocatum dabit uobis. post quae etiam illud subnectit: s quis me diligit, sermonem meum custodiet: et pater meus diliget illum, et ad eum ueniemus, et mansionem apud illum Jaciemus. nec non etiam subdidit illud quoque: aduocatus autem ille spiritus sanctus, quem missurus est pater, ille uos docebit et commemorabit- omnia quaecumque dixero. praemittit adhuc istum locum, quo ostendat se esse filium, et merito subdidit, et dicit: s me diligeretis, gauderetis, quia eo ad patrem: quia pater maior me est. quid autem cum etiam ila subnectit: ego sum uitis uera, et pater meus agricola: omne sarmentum in me non afferens fructum tollit illud, et omne fructtSerum purgat, ut fructum ampliorem ferat? instat adhuc et adicit: sicut dilexit me pater, et ego dilexi uos; manete in mea caritate; si mandata mea seruaueritis, manebitis in mea caritale, sicut ego patris mandata seruaui, et maneo in eius caritate. adhuc ingerit, et dicit: dixi autem uos amicos, quia omnia quae audiui a patre meo, nota uobis feci. aggregat etiam hoc: sed haec omnia facient uobis propter nomen meum, quia ignorant eum qui me misit. Haec ergo numquam post illa euidenter illum non patrem sed filium esse testantia dominus subdidisset, si aut patrem se esse meminisset, aut patrem se uellet intellegi. nisi quoniam ut illud exprimeret, perinde unumquemque iam habere debere, dum imaginem dei patris per filium uidet, atque si uiderit patrem—quandoquidem unusquisque credens in filium exerceatur in imaginis contemplatione, ut assuefactus ad diuinitatem uidendam imagine proficere possit et crescere usque ad dei patris omnipotentis perfectam contemplationem,—et quoniam, qui hoc animo ac mentecombiberit et de omnibus sic futurum esse crediderit, patrem, quem uisurus sit, quasi iam quodammodo uiderit et hic iam sic habeat, quasi teneat, quod habiturum se pro certo sciat. Ceterum, si ipse pater fuisset, quid quasi futurum praemium repromittebat, quod iam praestiterat et dederat? nam quoniam dicit: beati mundo corde, quia ipsi deum uidebunt, polliceri deprehenditur contemplationem et aspectum patris. ergo nondum dederat: cur enim repromitteret, si iam dedisset? dederat enim, si pater esset; uidebatur enim, et contingebatur. quando autem, dum contingitur ipse Christus et uidetur, repromittit tamen et dicit, quoniam qui mundo fuerit corde, deum uidebit, hoc ipso probat patrem se non esse, qui tunc praesens cum uideretur repromittebat, quod patrem uisurus esset quisquis mundo corde fuisset. erat ergo repromittens haec non pater sed filius; quia qui filius erat, quod uideri habebat repromittebat: cuius repromissio superuacua fuisset, nisi filius fuisset. cur enim repromittebat mundis ut uiderent patrem, Si iam tunc qui praesentes erant, patrem Christum uidebant? sed quia filius erat, non pater, merito et filius, quia imago dei, tunc uidebatur, et pater, quia inuisibilis, mundis corde, ut uideretur, repromittitur et notatur. Haec igitur satis sit etiam aduersus istum haereticum dictasse, pauca de multis. campus enim, et quidem latus ac fusus, aperietur, plenius haereticum istum si agitare uoluerimus; quandoquidem duobus istis locis quibusdam effossis luminibus orbatus, totus sit in doctrinae suae caecitate superatus.
thought_title: Christ is the Son, not the Father
pass_a_gloss: I will add also that part in which, while the heretic, as it were, rejoices with a certain eye, having lost the truth and light, may recognize the total blindness of his error. For he frequently opposes the fact that it was said: I am with you in healthy times, and you do not recognize me? Philip, who saw me, saw also the Father. But what he does not understand, let him learn. Philip is blamed, and rightly and deservedly, because he said: Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us. For when did he hear or learn from Christ that Christ was the Father, since, on the contrary, he heard and learned more frequently that He was the Son, not the Father? For what the Lord said, If you have known me, you have known my Father, and from now on you know Him, and you have seen Him, He did not say in such a way that He wanted to be understood as the Father, but because whoever approaches the Son of God with total faith and total devotion will come to the Father through the Son, in whom he believes, and will see Him. For no one, He says, can come to the Father except through me, and therefore he who comes to God the Father will not only come and know the Father, but also ought to hold and presume in his mind and heart as if he already knew and saw the Father. For divine Scripture, which announces things that have not yet been done as if they were already done, because they will be, and which will be in all ways, does not predict them as if they were future, but narrates them as if they were already done. Finally, when Christ had not yet been born in the time of the prophet Isaiah, it was said: A child is born to us; and when He had not yet come to Mary, it was said to the prophet: He came and she conceived and bore a son. And when Christ had not yet exposed His breast, it was said: His name will be called Angel of great counsel. And when He had not yet suffered, it was proclaimed: He was led to slaughter. And when the cross did not yet exist, it was said: I have stretched out my hands all day to a disobedient people. And when He had not yet been given vinegar to drink, it was said: They gave me vinegar to drink. And when He had not yet been stripped, it was said: They cast lots for my garment, and they numbered my bones, and they pierced my hands and feet. For divine Scripture speaks of things that will be done as if they were already done, and of things that will be perfect as if they were already perfect, which will come without doubt. And therefore the Lord said in this place: From now on you know Him, and you have seen Him. For He said that the Father would be seen by whoever followed the Son; not that the Son Himself was the Father seen, but that whoever followed Him and wanted to be His disciple would receive the reward of seeing the Father. For the Son is the image of God the Father, so that it may be added that, just as the Father works, so also the Son works, and the Son is the imitator of all the Father's works; so that each one may have it, as if he had already seen the Father, while seeing Him who always imitates the invisible Father in all His works. But if Christ Himself were the Father, how could He immediately add and say: He who believes in me will do the works that I do, and greater works than these will he do, because I am going to the Father? And He also adds: If you love me, keep my commandments; and I will ask the Father, and He will give you another Advocate. And after these things, He also adds: He who loves me will keep my word; and my Father will love him, and we will come to him, and we will make our abode with him. And He also adds: The Advocate is the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send, and He will teach you and remind you of all that I have said. He anticipates this place, where He shows Himself to be the Son, and rightly adds, saying: If you loved me, you would rejoice, because I am going to the Father; for the Father is greater than I. And what about when He also adds: I am the true vine, and my Father is the farmer; every branch in me that does not bear fruit, He takes away, and every fruitful branch He purifies, that it may bear more fruit? He also says: As the Father loved me, I also loved you; remain in my love; if you keep my commandments, you will remain in my love, just as I have kept my Father's commandments and remain in His love. He also says: I have called you friends, because all that I heard from my Father, I have made known to you. He also adds: They will do all these things to you on account of my name, because they do not know Him who sent me. The Lord would not have added these things, which clearly testify that He is not the Father but the Son, if He had remembered that He was the Father or wanted to be understood as the Father. Unless it is because He wanted to express that each one ought to have it, as if he had already seen the Father, while seeing the image of God the Father through the Son, and as if he had seen the Father, since each believer in the Son is exercised in the contemplation of the image, so that, having become accustomed to seeing the divinity in the image, he may progress and grow until he reaches the perfect contemplation of God the Father, Almighty. But if Christ Himself were the Father, what reward would He promise as if it were future, which He had already given and bestowed? For since He says: Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God, He is found to promise the contemplation and vision of the Father. Therefore, He had not yet given it; why would He promise it, if He had already given it? For if He were the Father, He would have been seen and touched. But when Christ, while being touched and seen, still promises and says that whoever is pure in heart will see God, He proves by this that He is not the Father, who, being present and seen, promises that whoever is pure in heart will see the Father. Therefore, it was not the Father but the Son who promised these things; because, being the Son, He promised what He had to be seen: whose promise would have been superfluous if He were not the Son. Why would He promise to the pure in heart that they would see the Father, if those who were present were already seeing Christ as the Father? But because He was the Son, not the Father, and the Son is the image of God, He was seen, and the Father, being invisible, is promised to be seen by the pure in heart. These things, therefore, are enough to have been said against this heretic, even if only a few of many things. For if we wanted to discuss this heretic more fully, a wide and extensive field would be opened, since, having been blinded by the removal of two passages, he is completely overcome by the blindness of his doctrine.

pass_b_english: I must also address the section where the heretic thinks he sees clearly but has actually lost all truth and light, so that he may finally recognize the total blindness of his error. He repeatedly throws up the words: "I have been with you for a long time, and still you do not know me? Philip, whoever has seen me has seen the Father" (John 14:9). He needs to learn what he fails to understand. Philip is rebuked, and justly so, because he said, "Lord, show us the Father, and that will be enough for us." When had Philip ever heard or learned from Christ that Christ was the Father? On the contrary, he had heard and learned far more often that He was the Son, not the Father. When the Lord said, "If you had known me, you would have known my Father also; from now on you know him and have seen him" (John 14:7), He did not mean to be understood as the Father Himself. He meant that whoever approaches the Son of God with total faith and total devotion will come to the Father through the Son in whom he believes, and will see Him. Jesus said, "No one comes to the Father except through me" (John 14:6). Therefore, the one who comes to God the Father will not only come to know Him, but ought also to hold fast in mind and heart as if he already knows and sees the Father. Divine Scripture often announces things not yet done as if they were already accomplished, because they are certain to happen. It does not merely predict them as future; it narrates them as already fulfilled. Long before Christ was born in Isaiah's time, it was said, "A child is born to us" (Isaiah 9:6). Before He came to Mary, the prophet was told, "Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son" (Isaiah 7:14). Before Christ revealed the Father's heart, it was said, "His name shall be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God" (Isaiah 9:6). Before He suffered, it was proclaimed, "He was led like a lamb to the slaughter" (Isaiah 53:7). Before the cross existed, God said, "All day long I have held out my hands to a disobedient people" (Isaiah 65:2; Romans 10:21). Before He was given vinegar, it was written, "They gave me vinegar for my thirst" (Psalm 69:21). Before He was stripped, it was said, "They cast lots for my garment" (Psalm 22:18), "They numbered my bones" (Psalm 22:17), "They pierced my hands and feet" (Psalm 22:16). Divine Scripture speaks of future events as accomplished, and of future perfections as already perfect, because their coming is beyond doubt. That is why the Lord said in this passage, "From now on you know him and have seen him" (John 14:7). He declared that the Father would be seen by anyone who followed the Son — not that the Son Himself was the Father seen, but that the reward for following Him and becoming His disciple would be the vision of the Father. The Son is the image of God the Father (John 14:9; Colossians 1:15), so that, just as the Father works, so also the Son works, and the Son imitates all the Father's works (John 5:19). Thus each person may have it as if he had already seen the Father, while seeing the One who always imitates the invisible Father in every work. But if Christ Himself were the Father, how could He immediately add, "Whoever believes in me will do the works I do, and greater works than these will he do, because I am going to the Father" (John 14:12)? And He goes on: "If you love me, keep my commandments. And I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Advocate" (John 14:15–16). Then: "If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our home with him" (John 14:23). And: "The Advocate, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, will teach you all things and remind you of everything I have said" (John 14:26). He anticipates this passage to show He is the Son, and rightly adds: "If you loved me, you would rejoice that I am going to the Father, for the Father is greater than I" (John 14:28). What about when He also says: "I am the true vine, and my Father is the gardener. Every branch in me that bears no fruit he takes away, and every branch that does bear fruit he prunes, that it may bear more fruit" (John 15:1–2)? He insists: "As the Father has loved me, so have I loved you. Abide in my love. If you keep my commandments, you will abide in my love, just as I have kept my Father's commandments and abide in his love" (John 15:9–10). He also says: "I have called you friends, for all that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you" (John 15:15). And He adds: "They will do all these things to you on account of my name, because they do not know the one who sent me" (John 15:21). The Lord would never have appended these words, which plainly testify that He is not the Father but the Son, if He had thought of Himself as the Father or wanted to be understood as the Father — unless He meant to express that each believer ought to possess, as if he had already seen the Father, the vision of God's image through the Son. For everyone who believes in the Son is exercised in contemplating that image, so that, growing accustomed to seeing the divine through the image, he may advance and grow until he reaches the perfect contemplation of God the Father Almighty. Since the one who embraces this with mind and heart, believing all this will come to pass, already possesses in a real sense the Father he will one day see, and already holds as certain what he knows he will obtain. But if Christ were the Father, what future reward would He promise that He had already given and bestowed? He says, "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God" (Matthew 5:8). He thereby promises the contemplation and vision of the Father. So He had not yet given it; why promise what is already given? If He were the Father, He would have been seen and touched. Yet while Christ was being touched and seen, He still promised that the pure in heart would see God. This proves He is not the Father — the One who, though present and visible, promised that the pure in heart would see the Father. Therefore, it was the Son, not the Father, who made this promise. As the Son, He promised what He had yet to be seen: a promise that would have been pointless if He were not the Son. Why promise the pure in heart that they would see the Father, if those present were already seeing Christ as the Father? But because He was the Son, not the Father, and the Son is the image of God, He was seen then, while the Father — being invisible — is promised to the pure in heart as the one they will see. This is enough said against this heretic, though it is only a few points out of many. A broad and extensive field would open if we wished to engage him more fully. Deprived of the light from these two passages, he is completely overcome by the blindness of his own doctrine.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text, including the complex theological arguments regarding the distinction between the Son and the Father and the nature of prophetic fulfillment. Scripture citations in Pass B are correctly added to the text to identify the quoted/alluded passages (e.g., John 14:7, Isaiah 9:6, etc.) and match the content. The title 'Christ is the Son, not the Father' correctly names the thought of the chapter.
